To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the superior cervical ganglia from newborn and young rats contain a population of multipotential neurons which can differentiate into cholinergic or adrenergic neurons, and that the differentiation along cholinergic or noradrenergic lines is accompanied by the acquisition of a specific pattern of enzyme activities.
The superior cervical ganglion contains neurons that are able to differentiate along either adrenergic, cholinergic or mixed adrenergic-cholinergic lines.

the choline acethyltransferase activity in the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion of the newborn rat increases with age in vivo and in culture in the absence of added nerve growth factor, but the tyrosine hydroxyylase activity decreases in culture in the presence or absence of nerve growth factors, and the choline acetytransferase activity increases with age in the newborn rat in the presence of high concentrations of nerve growth factors.

the development of the superior cervical ganglia of the rat in the presence of nerve growth factor, guanethidine, and anti-nerve-growth-factor.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the development of the superior cervical ganglia of rats is a dynamic process in which the balance of the various influences on neuronal development changes with time.
the superior cervical ganglia contain multipotential cells which, under appropriate circumstances, can differentiate into adrenergic neurons or cholinergic neurons.
nerve growth factor has an important role in the survival, differentiation and maintenance of sympathetic neurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the newborn rat the ganglia contains a large number of multipotential cells which have not yet committed themselves to a particular neurotransmitter phenotype.
nerve growth factor has a dual role in the development of the sympathetic neuron.

the presence of high concentrations of nerve growth factors (e.g., 1 μg/g in vivo or 1 μg/ ml in vitro ) is sufficient to maintain the differentiated state of both noradrenergic and cholinergic neurons, whereas the presence of low concentrations of nerve growth fact or (e.g., less than 0.1 μg/g or 0.1μg/ml) is sufficient to maintain only the differentiated state of noradrenerg ic neurons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of a multipotiental cell type is a prerequisite for the development of a sympathetic ganglion.
there is a multipotential precursor in the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion that is responsive to both nerve growth factor and guanethidine.

the superior cervical ganglia of the rat are not a good model for studying the effects of nerve growth factor on sympathetic neuron differentiation because they already contain neurons which are differentiated along cholinergic and adrenergic lines.
